items.note: Six-line inscription on the right side of the temple's east doorway records Vaishakh Sudi 7, Vikram Samvat 1137, worked out as 30 March 1080.
Records the temple's flag-hoisting; of about a dozen inscriptions found at Udaipur this one, of 1080 and Udayaditya's time, is the oldest and most important.
Inscription names its composer, Pandit Mahipal, son of Pandit Shringavas.
Author says the temple took more than twenty years to build and make ready.
INTACH has traced more than a hundred inscriptions in Udaipur alone.
Santosh Kumar Verma: inscription of Vikram Samvat 1137, Vaishakh Sudi 7; no weekday given; calculated as Monday 30 March 1080 CE.
Verma: this inscription's date is the first recorded date of Udayaditya's reign, which the other inscriptions lack.
Sanskrit in eleventh-century Nagari script, prose-dominant, with one shloka in Anushtubh metre.
Composer Pandit Mahipala son of Pandit Shringavas; sixth line says Maharaja Udayaditya completed the flag-hoisting of the Shri Udayeshvardev temple.
Countless inscriptions flank the temple's eastern gate; one upper-left inscription shows the name 'Shriman Udayadityanripati'.
Translation of line 1: 'May King Udayadity make the earth [united] under a single umbrella'.
Date line: Samvat 1137, Vaishakh Sudi 7.
Translation of final line: the flag-hoisting of Shrimat Udayeshvar Dev was completed.
Author notes the inscription has long been in the ASI's records.

Earlier notices of the 1080 inscription: Cunningham, ASI Report vol. 10 p. 83 (1880); D. R. Bhandarkar, Progress Report Western Circle 1913-14 p. 22; M. B. Garde, Gwalior State Annual Report Samvat 1974.
refs: Bhandarkar, Progress Report of the Archaeological Survey, Western Circle, 1913-14, p. 22
Garde, Annual Report of the Archaeological Department in Gwalior State, Samvat 1974

items.note: Proposal: display Hindi and English translations of the inscriptions in large clear letters, ideally carved on local quarry stone.
Second temple inscription: VS 1116 and Shak 981 (1059 CE); 22 lines, error-ridden, begins with worship of Shiva then turns to Udayaditya.
Verses 2-5 as rendered: Paramara king; son Gandal; his son Pata (Jnata) built temples with reservoirs; he deemed Udayaditya worthy and made him king.
Verma: naming Pata/Jnata as father suggests Udayaditya came from a junior branch, not Sindhuraja's line, and perhaps ruled eastern Malwa, including Vidisha, as a feudatory under Bhoj.

claim.value: junior branch of the Paramaras; possibly feudatory (samantadhipati) under Bhoj (Verma)

items.note: Verma: around 1070 CE Bhoj's son and successor Jaisingh I was killed in battle, creating a political vacuum in which Udayaditya may have come to the throne.
Shorgadh inscription lines 5-6 call Udayaditya the padanudhyata of Bhojdev.
Padanudhyata used of Chandragupta II's commanders suggests literal 'meditating on the feet', a eulogy not succession; so the Shorgadh claim that Udayaditya succeeded Bhoj directly is weakened.

claim.value: padanudhyata is praise, not succession (Verma's argument)

items.note: Udaipur Prashasti gives the most detailed account of the Paramara dynasty up to Udayaditya and was got prepared by Udayaditya.
Translation of Prashasti verse 21: after Bhoj's departure to heaven and enemy darkness over the earth, Udayadityadev rose like the sun with his sword.

claim.value: rose after Bhoj's death (verse 21), relation unstated

items.note: Nagpur Prashasti of Narvarman verse 32: after Bhoj's passing his bandhu (kinsman) Udayaditya became king, rescuing the earth from Karnata, Karna and others.
Nagpur inscription of Narvarman, son of Udayaditya, who ruled 1094 to 1133 CE; composed by Narvarman himself (verse 56).
Jainad inscription of Jagdev, verse 6: his father was Udayaditya and Bhojraj was his pitrivya (paternal uncle).

claim.value: Bhoj was Jagdev's paternal uncle (Jainad inscription), so Udayaditya's brother

items.note: Dongargaon inscription of Jagdev, verse 5: after Bhoj, his brother Udayadity rose to eminence, rescuing Malava; Jainad says uncle, Dongargaon says brother.
Jagdev was the third and youngest son of Udayadity; Lakshmadeva died in his father's lifetime; Narvarman became the next ruler.
If Bhoj and Udayadity were uterine brothers: Bhojdev is a king at Dhar in 1011 CE and died in 1055 CE, so why did Udayadity wait until 1070 CE?
Historiography: Kielhorn held they were brothers; D. C. Ganguly cites the Ain-i-Akbari in favour; H. C. Ray, Dynastic History of Northern India, denies bandhu means brother.
refs: H. C. Ray, Dynastic History of Northern India

items.note: Undated Udayaditya-era inscription of 27 lines, found in a house in the Chatua Darwaza locality, now in the Gwalior Archaeology Museum.
Entirely Sanskrit verse, worn; published in the Gwalior State Annual Report 1925-26, serial no. 71, pp. 12-13.
refs: Annual Report of the Archaeological Department in Gwalior State, 1925-26, no. 71, pp. 12-13

items.note: First six lines describe Udayadity's victories; the only name given is the Chedi ruler of Dahalamandala, said to be defeated and killed; Dahal is the Jabalpur region, home of the Kalachuris.
Verma: the name ties Udaipur to Udayadity and no earlier Paramara inscription is found, so the town came into existence in Udayadity's time.

claim.value: Udayaditya (inferred from name and absence of earlier inscriptions)

items.note: In Vidisha district Jaisingh is probably the first Paramara ruler with a record; the genealogy there goes only up to Udayadityadev.

Inscription names Nemak-line Shiva-worshipping local rulers, possibly Rudraditya, and a feudatory Shudrak whose unnamed son had the Udaipur temple built; author surmises this family supervised construction.

claim.value: son of feudatory Shudrak of the Nemak line (name unclear), per undated inscription

items.note: Paramara evidence also lies in Padmagupta's Navasahasanka Charita and Merutunga's Prabandha Chintamani.
Udaipur Prashasti: fragmentary, found in the courtyard of the Nilkantheshvar temple, now in Gwalior museum; Sanskrit in eleventh-century Nagari; undated but of Udayadity's time.

claim.value: found in temple courtyard, now Gwalior museum; undated, fragmentary, Udayaditya's time

items.note: Udayadity's reign lay between 1070 and 1093.

When Pratihara power weakened the Kalachuris, Chandelas and Paramaras rose; Paramara kingdom ran from Malwa up to Vidisha and Udaipur beyond Bhopal, with branches at Chandravati, Bhinmal, Kiradu, Jalore and Bagar.
Udaipur Prashasti printed in Cunningham's reports and by Buhler in Epigraphia Indica vol. 1 (1888).
Translation of verse 1: invocation of Shambhu with the crescent moon and serpent garland.
Prashasti verse 5: on Mount Arbund a hero arose from the fire-pit (agnikund) by Vashishtha's power and destroyed the enemy army.
Verse 6: the sage said to the hero 'You shall be a king by the name of Paramar'.
Verse 7: Upendraraja arose in that dynasty and won exalted kingship by valour.
Verse 8: his son Bairisimha set up victory-pillars.
Verse 9: Shri Siyaka, foremost among victorious kings.
Verse 10: Shri Vakyapati, whose war-steeds drank the waters of the Ganga and the ocean.
Verse 11: Bairisimha, also called Vajratasvami, through whom the city of Dhara was brought to renown.
Verse 12: Shri Harshadeva seized the fortune of Khodingdev in battle.
Verse 13: Vakyapatirajadeva, accomplished in oratory, poetry, logic, shastra and agama.
Verse 14: his feet tinted by the crown-jewels of the Karnata, Lata, Kerala and Chola kings.
Verse 15: desiring victory over Tripuri, he defeated the Yuvaraja and slew his commanders.
Verse 16: his younger brother Sindhuraja vanquished the Huna king; from him was born Bhojraja.
Verse 18: praise of Bhoj as poet-king (Kaviraja); what he accomplished, ordained, gave and knew, no other could do.
Verse 19: armies of the Karnata, Lata, Gurjar king, Turks and the Chedi king and others were conquered by his mere servants.
Verse 20: he built temples of Kedareshvar, Rameshvar, Somnath, Sundir, Kala, Anal, Rudra and the rest.
Verse 21 translation: after Bhoj's departure and enemy darkness over Dhara, Udayadityadev rose like the sun gladdening the people.
Verse 22: Udayaditya accomplished the earth-lifting of the Varaha avatar with ease.
Says this is the most important of the Udaipur inscriptions; in the same series a total of 11 inscriptions are found from Udaipur on political, economic and social conditions.
Clean translations of the inscriptions should be available in the temple precinct for villagers and tourists.
Saraswati Kanthabharanas of Paramara times were knowledge-centres; the hostel at Mandu's one had an in-charge named Govind Bhatt.
Verma: akshayanivi endowments appear in the Satavahana period; after the Gupta period land grants to temples were large and carried special privileges.
Author infers Udaipur's temple budget must have been considerable; no writing gives detailed information on its economy.
Pillar inscription right of the temple's eastern gate records a devadeya; listed in Indian Antiquary vols 18 and 20, Gwalior Annual Report no. 121, Bhandarkar no. 483, Kielhorn no. 207.
refs: Indian Antiquary vol. 18, p. 342; vol. 20, p. 83
Annual Report, Gwalior State, Samvat 1974, no. 121
Bhandarkar, List of Northern Inscriptions, no. 483

items.note: Pillar inscription: 14 lines, Sanskrit, thirteenth-century Nagari, crude letters, broken corner and worn text.
Dated Samvat 1286 (1229 CE), Kartik Sudi, Friday; treasury officer Dhamdev donated 4 biswa of land to the temple of Udayeshvardev in Maharaja Devpaldev's reign.
Devpaldev styled only Mahakumar in the record; author infers he held a role in Udaipur before becoming king, as Udayadity may have, making Udaipur a source of two Paramara kings.
Four biswa is the twentieth part of a bigha, a very small plot; the unit was locally used in the Bhopal region.
Translation of line 11: taking water in hand, he donated 4 biswa (text damaged).
Translation of line 8: 'in the affair, the panchakula Shri Dhamdev ...' (damaged).
Verma: 'panchakul' in line 8 was often the village-elders' assembly, like a panchayat handling local administration.
Verma: such small parcels were also donated to temples elsewhere, in writings of the Chauhans of Nadol and Shakambhari and the Chalukyas of Gujarat.
Author speculates the 4 biswa plot may have held a water source, a stepwell or housing for the priest (conjecture, not documented).
Proposal to the ASI Regional Director in March 2021: display Hindi-English translations of selected inscriptions in the temple precinct.
Suggests posting skilled, interested staff at such sites rather than unskilled labour.
INTACH deployed an expert team that combed Udaipur, identified remnants of every ruler over 1000-1200 years, counted and documented the inscriptions.
The Nilkantheshvar temple is recorded in inscriptions as the Udayeshvar temple; the name Nilkantheshvar appears in no contemporary inscription; when it became famous is unknown.
Around a hundred inscriptions survive, in Sanskrit, Persian and Devanagari, some with Sanskrit and Persian together.
INTACH's ground work identified 42 new monuments needing care; five or six ancient stepwells survive in much better condition.
Jain idols on the hilly rocks show the region held religious traditions of every kind.
INTACH's plan: bring together ASI, State Archaeology Department, district administration, panchayat, private institutions and local society.
Upadhyay: panchayat-level documentation, as INTACH does in 10-12 districts, would bring many priceless things to knowledge.
Upadhyay: inscriptions are present here in large numbers; in the temple alone a whole PhD could be done on them.
Upadhyay: Madhya Pradesh has a famine of experts who can read inscriptions, even in government departments and educational institutions.
